Dear bloggers,
 
I am working with fertility schedules and I would like to interpolate each schedule with a spline curve and obtain certain values from the interpolated curve (such as the maximum and the flexes). Nevertheless, I haven't been able to come up with a code to do so... Anyone could please help me with this problem?
 
Thank you for any suggestion,
 
Ale
 
p <- ggplot(f_1_ISL, aes(EDAD,value))
p + geom_point(aes(colour=prov_geo), size = 1) +
       stat_smooth(colour="green",method = "glm",formula = y ~ ns(x,df=8)) +
       scale_colour_manual("Province", values=c("#000000", "#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73", "#F0E442", "#0072B2", "#D55E00", "#CC79A7","#003333","#33FFF3"))+
       labs(title = "Age Specific Fertility Schedules for ...",
  x = "", y = "") +
       geom_vline(xintercept=max(), col="red",linetype="dotdash")+
       theme(axis.text     = element_text(colour="grey", size=6, angle=0,
 face = "plain"),
 axis.text.x  = element_text(hjust=.5, vjust=.5),
 axis.text.y  = element_text(hjust=1, vjust=0),
 strip.text.x  = element_text(size = 8, colour = "black", angle = 0), plot.title      =       element_text(size=20)) +
  facet_wrap(~ year)

parts:
Thank you Dennis for your suggestions, it is all much clearer now. I have one more question.
When you suggest to "to fit the curves in ggplot2... but to use the spline model objects to extract the knots and extrema, summarize them appropriately in a data frame... and then import it when you want to add layers to a ggplot that utilizes this information." I am not sure I get what you mean. This is what I came up with but I am not sure it is the best&most efficient solution:
 
having this inside my ggplot code:
 stat_smooth(colour="green",method = "lm",formula = y ~ ns(x,df=8))
 
and then
lm.prov <- lm(f_1_ISL$value~ns(f_1_ISL$EDAD,df=8))
summary(lm.prov)
 
 
Ale
 


2013/5/7 Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com>
Hi:

Firstly, y ~ ns(x, df = 8) is a linear model, not a GLM. Spline fits
use more general basis functions for the model matrix, but it's still
a linear model. Secondly, if you want to extract features from the
curves, it's probably better to do the model fitting outside of
ggplot2, determine what you need from the curves and summarize it in a
data frame separate from the input data. I'm assuming that what you
mean by the 'flexes' are the knots of the spline.

The maxima and minima, along with their locations, can be found
approximately with max/which.max and min/which.min, respectively, or
perhaps a little more accurately by taking numerical derivatives of
the fitted splines and finding their zeros with a root-finding
function. (This is all outside of ggplot2, BTW.) The knots are likely
to be found in the fitted spline object.

ggplot2 selects 80 equally spaced points between min(x) and max(x) in
the data, fits the curve at those points and plots it. That
information is recorded and accessed by saving the ggplot to an object
and then calling ggplot_build() on it, where you'll find what was
plotted in the first list component named data. It does not save the
remaining output from the spline fit, however - it only saves the
locations it created and the predicted values from the spline model at
those points. There is no guarantee that the extrema of the curve will
be accurately conveyed in the ggplot2 fit, although it will usually be
close.

Given the type of information you want from the spline model, it's
better to fit it outside of ggplot2. Since you have a grouping
variable, you can create a list of model fits and extract what you
need from them with lapply() or a list-related function from the plyr
package (e.g., ldply() or llply()). Since each geom_ function takes a
data = argument, you can use different data frames in different layers
of a ggplot. This is one of its strengths as a package.

A compromise of sorts is to fit the curves in ggplot2 (especially if
you want to use the confidence bounds of the separate curves) but to
use the spline model objects to extract the knots and extrema,
summarize them appropriately in a data frame (including year, since
you're faceting) and then import it when you want to add layers to a
ggplot that utilizes this information.

Dennis

parts:
I have attached the gist file containing all the information (it's a subset of the whole dataset as it would be a bit too long, but it's representative anyway).
 
My persisting problem is that I cannot really manage to find the points I want on the smoothed curve:
 
lm.prov <- lm(m$EDAD~ns(m$value, df=8)
 
should produce a smoothing curve, but I cannot really work out the fact that I have different years to take into consideration as well as different provinces (variable 'year' and variable 'prov_num')
For instance, I would like to get the max of the curve, but I find this:
 
max(fitted.values(lm.prov))
[1] 47.20899
 
For me it would be good to produce a dataframe containing all the global maximum and the knots for each province and each year.
I hope I have been clear enough. It would be a great step ahead for my analysis to have some help on the matter.
 
 
Ale
 
2013/5/7 Dennis Murphy <djm...@gmail.com>
You need to find the information you want from lm.prov, extract it and
put it into a data frame. You can then use that data frame as the
input data for one or more layers of a ggplot. If you provide a
reproducible example to the ggplot2 group with an explanation of what
you want, it will become clearer what I mean.

Please provide a reproducible example:
https://github.com/hadley/devtools/wiki/Reproducibility

Dennis
